title: Your Own Evidence
titleHtml: The standard shows up in your evidence.
tagline: Evidence of the manager standard: what gets measured.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for Vanderbilt managers: see how the manager standard is measured through demonstrated behavior, read your own pulse and cadence evidence without flinching, and choose one behavior to make more visible this month.
heroLead: The manager standard stopped being a poster this year. It is measured now, through what pulse data, 1:1 cadence, and team signals actually show. This session teaches you to read your own evidence calmly and pick one behavior to make more visible.
objectives: Name the three evidence streams that measure the manager standard
Read your own pulse and cadence data without a defensive story
Choose one leader behavior to make more visible this month
missionTie: Defining the great university of the 21st Century takes leadership you can actually see. Measured leader behavior turns good management into Exceptional Core Operations, one visible habit at a time.
goalLead: Goal 2 promised a manager standard that measures demonstrated behavior. This month the measurement is live, and today you learn to read what it says about you.

agenda.d: The three evidence streams: pulse data, 1:1 cadence, and team signals.
Your evidence is information about behavior. Defensiveness turns it into an argument.
Pick one behavior and make it easy to see, and easy to measure, this month.

manifesto: You do not get to grade your own leadership anymore. The evidence does.

sections.headline: The standard is measured in behavior.
sections.lead: The manager standard is a list of behaviors, and behaviors leave traces. Pulse scores show how your team experiences you. 1:1 cadence shows whether the conversations happen. Team signals, like retention and growth, show what it all adds up to.
sections.group: In pairs: which of the three streams do you check least, and what might it be saying right now? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name the evidence stream you check least, and write one guess at what it says right now.

card.text: Intentions are invisible; behavior is measurable. The standard tracks what you demonstrably do: the pulse your team answers, the 1:1s that happen or slip, and the signals your team sends with their feet and their growth.

interaction.context: Every manager on this call is already generating all three streams. Your team answered the last pulse. Your calendar holds the record of 1:1s held, moved, or quietly dropped. And over time, retention and growth tell their own story. None of it needs a new tool; it needs a reader.
interaction.discuss: Which stream would surprise you most if you looked today, and what has kept it the one you check least?
interaction.q: Quick check: which of these counts as evidence of the manager standard?

opts.t: How much you care about your team
opts.why: Caring matters, and it stays invisible until it becomes behavior. The standard measures the demonstration, so care has to show up as something a team can experience.

opts.t: Your 1:1s happening on cadence, month after month
opts.why: Exactly. A held 1:1 is demonstrated behavior: visible, countable, and felt by the person on the other side of it.

opts.t: Your own rating of your leadership
opts.why: Self-ratings run famously generous. The standard reads the team's experience and the record of what happened, which is why the evidence can surprise you.

deeper.title: Reading the three streams together
deeper.body: Any single stream can mislead you for a quarter. A pulse dips during a reorg, cadence slips during a crunch, and a departure can be pure opportunity for the person leaving. The honest read is triangulation: when two streams point the same direction for two cycles running, treat it as signal. One stream, one cycle is a prompt to keep watching, never a conclusion.
steps: In a private note, capture all three streams: your last pulse result, your 1:1 record for the past two months, and any team moves over the past year.
Mark where two streams agree. That agreement is your strongest signal, and the behavior it points at is your best candidate for this month.
Put a recurring 15-minute hold on your calendar to reread all three monthly; the read only works as a habit.

sections.headline: Evidence is information, once you stop arguing with it.
sections.lead: A dip in your pulse score is a data point about how the team experienced the quarter. The defensive move explains it away; the overcorrection turns it into a verdict on you. The evidence read asks one question: what behavior would move this number?
sections.group: Pairs: name one piece of manager feedback you argued with at first. What was the evidence read? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Recall one piece of feedback you argued with at first. Write the evidence read you could have made instead.

interaction.intro: Three managers meet their own evidence. Call each reaction: an evidence read, a defensive read, or an overcorrection.
interaction.passMsg: You can hear the difference. Evidence earns one behavior change; defensiveness gets dropped; overcorrection gets perspective.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: an evidence read asks what behavior would move the number. Defensiveness argues with the data; overcorrection makes it a verdict.

items.q: Pulse dips on 'my manager gives useful feedback.' The manager thinks: the survey ran during crunch, so it does not count.
items.why: The timing may be real context, and 'it does not count' is the tell. A defensive read closes the question the data just opened.

items.q: The 1:1 record shows the manager cancelled four of the last six. Their read: that is my behavior, and cadence is the fix.
items.why: That is the evidence read: a countable behavior, owned without drama, answered with one concrete change the team will feel.

items.q: One pulse comment says meetings run long. The manager cancels every recurring meeting and rebuilds the team calendar overnight.
items.why: One comment earned one adjustment. Rebuilding everything overnight treats a signal as a verdict, and it usually creates the next problem.

deeper.title: The second draft rule
deeper.body: The defensive story is not a character flaw; it is the first draft everyone writes when their own numbers sting. The discipline is refusing to act on the first draft. Sit with stinging data for a day, then write the evidence read in one sentence: the behavior this points at is X. If context genuinely explains the number, write the context down too, and still pick a behavior. Context and behavior can both be true.
steps: Find one number or comment from the past year that still annoys you. Write the defensive story you told first, word for word.
Under it, write the one-sentence evidence read: what behavior would move this?
Note which draft you actually acted on at the time, and what the second draft would have changed.

sections.headline: Pick one behavior. Make it easy to see.
sections.lead: The standard rewards behavior a team can actually observe. So choose one behavior your evidence points at, then make it visible on purpose: named to your team, put on the calendar, and easy to catch you doing.

interaction.intro: Your evidence points at one behavior. Choose what you commit to and how the team will see it.

opts.coach: Nobody can see 'overall.' A behavior the standard can measure has a time, a place, and a witness.

opts.t: Give more feedback when I notice good work
opts.coach: Closer: it is a real behavior. 'When I notice' hides it from the calendar, so busy weeks will quietly delete it.

opts.t: Open every 1:1 with ten minutes on their growth, starting this week
opts.coach: Specific, scheduled, and observable. Your team can see it, your calendar can prove it, and the pulse can feel it.

opts.t: Just do it quietly and let people notice
opts.coach: Quiet virtue is real and unmeasurable. If nobody knows to look, the behavior can vanish for a month before anyone misses it.

opts.t: Mention it once at the next team meeting
opts.coach: Naming it helps. Once is a headline; the standard is looking for a pattern your team could describe a month from now.

opts.t: Name it to the team, calendar it, and ask them to call it if it slips
opts.coach: You just built your own measurement: a named commitment, a visible cadence, and a team deputized to keep you honest.

heads.strong: A behavior the standard can find. Your team can name it, your calendar can prove it, and May can measure it.
heads.mid: A real intention with weak visibility. The behavior may happen; the evidence of it is left to luck.
heads.weak: A private resolution. By month end it reads exactly like doing nothing, because nothing about it can be seen.

reactions.strong: Three weeks in, someone on your team mentions the growth minutes to a colleague without prompting. When the next pulse runs, the feedback question moves, and you know exactly which behavior moved it.
reactions.mid: The team half-remembers the announcement. Some weeks it happens, some it slips, and when the pulse runs you honestly cannot say whether the number reflects the change or the noise.
reactions.weak: You did try, some weeks. Nothing was named and nothing was scheduled, so the effort left no trace, and the next pulse reads it the only way it can: unchanged.

deeper.title: Designing the witness
deeper.body: Visibility fails quietly when nobody is assigned to notice. Borrow a trick from good goal design: name the witness, not just the behavior. Tell one specific person what to watch for and when to flag a slip; a deputized witness turns your busiest week from a loophole into a checkpoint. Then park the behavior where evidence already collects, inside the 1:1 or on the shared calendar, so proof accumulates without extra work.
steps: Write your one behavior as a sentence with a time and a place: I will do X at every Y.
Pick the witness: the team member or peer who will see it most often, and tell them this week what to watch for.
Check that your calendar could prove it later: recurring holds, agenda lines, anything that leaves a trace.

recap.q: How is the Vanderbilt manager standard measured?
opts: By managers rating their own leadership
Through demonstrated behavior: pulse, cadence, team signals
recap.why: The standard tracks what managers demonstrably do and what teams experience: pulse data, held 1:1s, and the signals a team sends over time.

recap.q: Your pulse score dips. The evidence read asks...
opts: How do I explain this away?
What behavior would move this number?
How fast can I change everything?
recap.why: Evidence is information about behavior. The productive question aims at one behavior change, without the defensive story or the overnight overcorrection.

recap.q: What makes a chosen behavior count toward the standard?
opts: Keeping it private so it stays humble
It is visible: named, scheduled, observable
recap.why: The standard reads what can be seen. Naming the behavior, putting it on a cadence, and letting the team observe it turns intent into evidence.

recapMsgs.high: You can read your own evidence. Now go pick the behavior it points at.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Reread the section you missed, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One behavior. In plain sight.
capstone.lead: Choose the behavior your evidence points at. Nothing you type is saved or sent; keep any team references to roles, never names.
capstone.whoLabel: Which evidence stream prompted this, and what did it show?
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. pulse feedback question dipped two quarters running
capstone.practiceLabel: Which behavior do you make visible?
capstone.whoRow: The evidence and what it showed

practices.name: The held 1:1
practices.move: Protect every 1:1 on the calendar this month; if one must move, it gets rebooked in the same week, never dropped.

practices.name: The feedback opener
practices.move: Open each 1:1 with ten minutes of real feedback and growth talk before any status updates.

practices.name: The named commitment
practices.move: Tell the team the one behavior you are working on and ask them to call it when it slips.

whens.out: The behavior starts this week and is named to the team by Friday.
The behavior debuts at your next scheduled 1:1 and holds for the rest of May.
The behavior runs the full month with a calendar footprint that can prove it happened.

capstone.evidenceRow: At month end, one line: what did the next round of evidence show?

closing.headline: Let the standard see you.
closing.lead: You leave with a read on your own evidence and one behavior chosen to make visible. The rest of the week gives everyone at Vanderbilt the same literacy: reading their own signal without flinching.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Name the behavior on your card
closing.nextBody: Tell your team the one behavior you are making visible this month and put it on the calendar. For a warm-up, the LinkedIn Learning course Giving and Receiving Feedback by Gemma Leigh Roberts has a navigator-led role-play worth twenty minutes first.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; May is month eight, when the manager standard becomes visible, and measurable.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Is the behavior on your card named to your team and on the calendar? What did your evidence show that surprised you? What will you check next month?' Count of named, scheduled behaviors is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: What gets measured
s1.purpose: Install the three evidence streams: pulse data, 1:1 cadence, and team signals.
s1.say: When this series first introduced the manager standard, it was a promise on a slide. This month it is a measurement. Here is the part that matters: it measures behavior, in three streams your team already generates. How they answer the pulse. Whether your 1:1s actually happen. The signals they send over time with retention and growth. Today is about reading those streams like a professional instead of like a defendant.
facilitate: Read the lead once, then walk the concept card and the In the room card together; no quiz in the live room.
Lead the discussion prompt aloud; take two or three voices, plus a chat vote on the least-checked stream.
Run the breakout on the least-checked stream, 90 seconds each way.

ask.q: Which of the three streams do you trust least, and why?
expect: Pulse, because scores feel noisy or unfair
Team signals, because they arrive slowly
ask.respond: Fair. Any one stream alone is noisy; the standard reads all three together, which is what makes the picture honest.

s1.debrief: Behavior leaves traces. The standard reads the traces, and so can you.
s1.watchFor: Managers debating survey methodology. Redirect: the streams are a mirror, and today's work is reading it; fixing the mirror is somebody else's job.
s1.transition: Reading the streams is easy on a good quarter. The skill shows up when the evidence stings.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; take the least-checked stream as a chat vote only.

s2.title: Reading without flinching
s2.purpose: Teach the evidence read: treating your own data as information about behavior, without defensiveness or overcorrection.
s2.say: Here is what happens to most of us when our own numbers dip: we become defense attorneys. The survey timing was bad, the team misread the question, that one person is grumpy. Every one of those might be true, and none of them moves the number. The evidence read is one discipline: when the data stings, ask what behavior would move it. That question keeps you a manager. The other questions turn you into a defendant.
facilitate: Run Call the read live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round one, pause: ask who sympathized with the defensive manager and why.
Run the breakout on feedback they argued with at first.

ask.q: What makes the overcorrection in round three feel virtuous?
expect: It proves you took the feedback seriously
ask.respond: Right, and that is the trap. One signal earns one adjustment. Dramatic overhauls are defensiveness wearing a cape.

s2.debrief: Defensiveness argues with the data. Overcorrection turns it into a verdict. The evidence read asks for one behavior.
s2.watchFor: Anyone spiraling on a real score they got. Normalize warmly: every manager in the room has a dip somewhere, and a dip is a prompt, never a verdict.
s2.transition: So your evidence points somewhere. Now you choose the behavior it points at.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

s3.title: One visible behavior
s3.purpose: Convert the evidence read into one named, scheduled, observable behavior for the month.
s3.say: The standard cannot measure your intentions, and honestly, neither can your team. So the move this month is almost mechanical: pick one behavior your evidence points at, then make it visible on purpose. Name it to your team. Put it on the calendar. Invite them to catch it slipping. Visibility feels like exposure, and it is actually insurance: a named behavior is one your busiest week cannot quietly delete.
facilitate: Run Make it visible; two minutes to choose both slots and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: named, scheduled, observable.

ask.q: Why does naming the behavior to your team feel risky?
expect: What if I slip in front of them
It sounds like a public promise
ask.respond: It is a public promise, and that is the design. A team that watches you keep a small promise learns the standard is real.

s3.debrief: Visible behavior has three parts: a name, a cadence, and witnesses.
s3.watchFor: Managers picking three behaviors. Cut them back to one; the month measures one thing well over three things vaguely.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your own card.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One behavior your evidence points at, one window to start it. Keep any team references to roles, never names. Build the card, copy it somewhere you will see it, and be ready to name the behavior to your team by Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave knowing how the standard reads you, and with one behavior about to become visible. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday opens the same toolbox for everyone: how the pulse and 360 tooling actually work and how to read your own signal. Thursday's Thrive Thursday goes a layer deeper with self-awareness and closing your blind spots. And if you want practice before you name your behavior, this month's LinkedIn Learning course, Giving and Receiving Feedback with Gemma Leigh Roberts, has a role-play you can run with its navigator in twenty minutes.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager shares a real pulse score and starts defending it to the room
contingencies.then: Protect and redirect: 'That number is yours, and this room is for the read: what behavior would move it?' Keep specifics private; the method is the lesson.

contingencies.if: Someone says the measurement is surveillance of managers
contingencies.then: Name what is measured: behaviors managers already owe their teams, read in aggregate over time. The standard watches patterns, and any manager can read their own evidence first.

toughQuestions.q: What if my pulse scores are bad because of things I can't control, like a reorg?
toughQuestions.a: Context is real, and the standard reads trends, so name the context and still pick a behavior. Teams in hard seasons rate managers on how visible and steady they were, and that part is fully yours.

toughQuestions.q: Doesn't making my behavior visible look like performing for the metric?
toughQuestions.a: Performing a held 1:1 requires holding the 1:1. The standard picks behaviors where the performance and the substance are the same act, which is why visibility is safe to lean into.

toughQuestions.q: Where does the LinkedIn Learning course fit? Is it required?
toughQuestions.a: It is optional and it is good: Giving and Receiving Feedback by Gemma Leigh Roberts, with a navigator-led feedback role-play and a development-plan build. Point managers to it as rehearsal for the conversation where they name their behavior.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on your own evidence. Bring a private guess: which of your numbers, pulse, 1:1 cadence, or team signals, would surprise you most? You will never be asked to share it. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Is the behavior visible yet? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Is the behavior on your card named to your team and on the calendar? 2) What did your evidence show that surprised you? 3) What will you check next month?
